**Holi**
A Hindu spring festival famous for participants throwing brightly colored powders and water balloons at one another. Bonfires lit on its eve (Holika Dahan) commemorate the boy Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, who survived unharmed when the demoness Holika, who was supposed to be immune to fire, sat with him in her lap in a fire and was burned herself. Drinks made from bhang (cannabis) are traditionally consumed during Holi.

**Diwali**
The Hindu "festival of lights," a five-day festival in which people light diyas (oil lamps) and lanterns. It commemorates Rama's return to Ayodhya after his fourteen-year exile in the forest and his defeat of the demon king Ravana. Gambling is considered auspicious during Diwali because of a story in which the goddess Parvati won a game of dice against Shiva.

**Kumbh Mela**
A massive Hindu pilgrimage held in a 12-year cycle, in which millions of pilgrims ritually bathe in sacred rivers. It rotates among four sites: Prayagraj (Allahabad) on the Ganges, Haridwar, Nashik on the Godavari, and Ujjain on the Shipra.

**Smarta tradition**
A Hindu tradition associated with the 8th-century philosopher Adi Shankara, which treats several deities as equal manifestations of the one Brahman. Its followers worship five deities, including the sun god Surya, a deity dating back to the Vedic period.

**Shaivism, Vaishnavism, and Shaktism**
The major denominations of Hinduism, centered respectively on Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars, and the Great Goddess (Mahadevi or Devi). The gods Brahma (the creator), Vishnu (the preserver), and Shiva (the destroyer) make up the Trimurti.

**Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, and Mahabharata**
Key Hindu scriptures. The Vedas are the oldest texts, the Upanishads are philosophical treatises about Brahman and the self, and the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata contains the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna.

**Laws of Manu**
The Manusmriti, an ancient Hindu law book that lays out social and religious duties, including the varnas (castes) and the shraddha rites performed for deceased ancestors. Members of the upper three varnas are called "twice-born" because of an initiation ceremony.

**Raksha Bandhan and rakhis**
A Hindu festival in which sisters tie protective threads or bracelets called rakhis around their brothers' wrists. In return, brothers promise to protect their sisters.

**Hindu temples (mandirs)**
Hindu temples are designed on square grids according to sacred architecture, with a 64-square grid among the most favored. South Indian temples have towering, sculpture-covered gateways called gopurams, the Konark Sun Temple features erotic sculptures, and Angkor Wat in Cambodia was originally built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu. The Swaminarayan Akshardham in Robbinsville, New Jersey claims to be one of the largest Hindu temples in the world.

**Rath Yatra and Jagannath**
A festival in Puri in which huge chariots carrying the deity Jagannath, a form of Krishna/Vishnu, and his siblings are pulled through the streets. Exaggerated claims that devotees threw themselves under the wheels gave English the word "juggernaut." The ISKCON (Hare Krishna) movement spread the festival worldwide.

**Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON)**
The International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in New York City in 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada. It is a Western-friendly branch of Vaishnavism known for chanting the sixteen-word Maha Mantra ("Hare Krishna, Hare Rama") and for its Food for Life charity.

**Four goals of life (purusharthas)**
The four aims of human life in Hinduism: dharma (duty and righteousness), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure), and moksha (liberation).

**Samsara, karma, and moksha**
Hindus believe in samsara, the cycle of rebirth, in which a person's karma (the moral consequences of actions) determines their next life, so someone with bad karma may be reborn as an animal. Moksha is liberation from this cycle.

**Samkhya and Yoga**
Two of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy. Samkhya, founded by the sage Kapila, holds a dualistic view of reality in which both prakriti (matter) and purusha (consciousness) are real, while Yoga uses physical postures called asanas and meditation.

**Four yugas**
Hinduism describes cosmic time as cycles of four ages, or yugas, which become progressively worse. The current age is the Kali Yuga, the dark or iron age.
